CausalChain: Gut microbiota dysbiosis -> Reduced activity of bile salt hydrolases and bile acid converting enzymes -> Lower conversion of primary bile acids to lithocholic acid -> Reduced activation of TGR5 in breast tissue -> Attenuated anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic signaling -> Increased breast cancer cell survival
Hypothesis: Enhancing the specific gut microbial conversion of primary bile acids to lithocholic acid will increase physiological TGR5 activation in breast tissue and promote tumor-suppressive signaling, thereby reducing breast cancer progression.
Abstract: This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the dual and context‐dependent roles that bile acids play in carcinogenic processes via receptor signaling and metabolic modulation. Building on the existing literature, we propose a hypothesis linking gut microbiome function with local breast tissue anti‐proliferative mechanisms. Specifically, we hypothesize that the microbial conversion of primary bile acids to tumor‐suppressive lithocholic acid (LCA) is critical for the activation of TGR5 receptor signaling in breast tissue. This activation promotes oxidative stress at a level that preferentially induces apoptosis in transformed epithelial cells while leaving non‐malignant cells unharmed. Thus, alterations in the gut microbial populations that diminish this conversion might contribute to breast cancer progression, and conversely, interventions to restore or enhance this conversion could serve as a preventive or therapeutic strategy.
